text: The Hanseatic League, commonly called The Hansa, was a medieval commercial and defensive network of merchant guilds and market towns in Central and Northern Europe.
en: The Hanseatic League, commonly called The Hansa, was a medieval commercial and defensive network of merchant guilds and market towns in Central and Northern Europe.

text: Growing from Lübeck and a few other North German towns in the late 12th century, the league expanded between the 13th and 15th centuries, ultimately encompassing nearly 200 settlements across eight modern-day countries, from Estonia and Russia in the northeast to the Netherlands in the west, with its inland extent reaching as far south as Cologne.
en: Growing from Lübeck and a few other North German towns in the late 12th century, the league expanded between the 13th and 15th centuries, ultimately encompassing nearly 200 settlements across eight modern-day countries, from Estonia and Russia in the northeast to the Netherlands in the west, with its inland extent reaching as far south as Cologne.

text: The league began as a collection of loosely associated groups of German traders and towns aiming to expand their commercial interests, including protection against robbery.
en: The league began as a collection of loosely associated groups of German traders and towns aiming to expand their commercial interests, including protection against robbery.

text: Over time, these arrangements evolved into the league, offering traders toll privileges and protection on affiliated territory and trade routes.
en: Over time, these arrangements evolved into the league, offering traders toll privileges and protection on affiliated territory and trade routes.

text: Economic interdependence and familial connections among merchant families led to deeper political integration and the reduction of trade barriers.
en: Economic interdependence and familial connections among merchant families led to deeper political integration and the reduction of trade barriers.

text: This gradual process involved standardizing trade regulations among Hanseatic cities.
en: This gradual process involved standardizing trade regulations among Hanseatic cities.

text: During its time, the Hanseatic League dominated maritime trade in the North and Baltic Seas.
en: During its time, the Hanseatic League dominated maritime trade in the North and Baltic Seas.

text: It established a network of trading posts in numerous towns and cities, notably the Kontors in London (known as the Steelyard), Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod, which became extraterritorial entities that enjoyed considerable legal autonomy.
en: It established a network of trading posts in numerous towns and cities, notably the Kontors in London (known as the Steelyard), Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod, which became extraterritorial entities that enjoyed considerable legal autonomy.

text: Hanseatic merchants operated private companies and were known for their access to commodities, and enjoyed privileges and protections abroad.
en: Hanseatic merchants operated private companies and were known for their access to commodities, and enjoyed privileges and protections abroad.

text: The league's economic power enabled it to impose blockades and even wage war against kingdoms and principalities.
en: The league's economic power enabled it to impose blockades and even wage war against kingdoms and principalities.

text: Even at its peak, the Hanseatic League remained a loosely aligned confederation of cities.
en: Even at its peak, the Hanseatic League remained a loosely aligned confederation of cities.

text: It lacked a permanent administrative body, a treasury, and a standing military force.
en: It lacked a permanent administrative body, a treasury, and a standing military force.

text: Photosynthesis is a system of biological processes by which photopigment-bearing autotrophic organisms, such as most plants, algae and cyanobacteria, convert light energy—typically from sunlight—into the chemical energy necessary to fuel their metabolism.
en: Photosynthesis is a system of biological processes by which photopigment-bearing autotrophic organisms, such as most plants, algae and cyanobacteria, convert light energy—typically from sunlight—into the chemical energy necessary to fuel their metabolism.

text: The term photosynthesis usually refers to oxygenic photosynthesis, a process that releases oxygen as a byproduct of water splitting.
en: The term photosynthesis usually refers to oxygenic photosynthesis, a process that releases oxygen as a byproduct of water splitting.

text: Photosynthetic organisms store the converted chemical energy within the bonds of intracellular organic compounds (complex compounds containing carbon), typically carbohydrates like sugars (mainly glucose, fructose and sucrose), starches, phytoglycogen and cellulose.
en: Photosynthetic organisms store the converted chemical energy within the bonds of intracellular organic compounds (complex compounds containing carbon), typically carbohydrates like sugars (mainly glucose, fructose and sucrose), starches, phytoglycogen and cellulose.

text: When needing to use this stored energy, an organism's cells then metabolize the organic compounds through cellular respiration.
en: When needing to use this stored energy, an organism's cells then metabolize the organic compounds through cellular respiration.

text: Photosynthesis plays a critical role in producing and maintaining the oxygen content of the Earth's atmosphere, and it supplies most of the biological energy necessary for complex life on Earth.
en: Photosynthesis plays a critical role in producing and maintaining the oxygen content of the Earth's atmosphere, and it supplies most of the biological energy necessary for complex life on Earth.

text: Some organisms also perform anoxygenic photosynthesis, which does not produce oxygen.
en: Some organisms also perform anoxygenic photosynthesis, which does not produce oxygen.

text: Some bacteria (e.g. purple bacteria) use bacteriochlorophyll to split hydrogen sulfide as a reductant instead of water, releasing sulfur instead of oxygen, which was a dominant form of photosynthesis in the euxinic Canfield oceans during the Boring Billion.
en: Some bacteria (e.g. purple bacteria) use bacteriochlorophyll to split hydrogen sulfide as a reductant instead of water, releasing sulfur instead of oxygen, which was a dominant form of photosynthesis in the euxinic Canfield oceans during the Boring Billion.

text: Archaea such as Halobacterium also perform a type of non-carbon-fixing anoxygenic photosynthesis, where the simpler photopigment retinal and its microbial rhodopsin derivatives are used to absorb green light and produce a proton (hydron) gradient across the cell membrane, and the subsequent ion movement powers transmembrane proton pumps to directly synthesize adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the "energy currency" of cells.
en: Archaea such as Halobacterium also perform a type of non-carbon-fixing anoxygenic photosynthesis, where the simpler photopigment retinal and its microbial rhodopsin derivatives are used to absorb green light and produce a proton (hydron) gradient across the cell membrane, and the subsequent ion movement powers transmembrane proton pumps to directly synthesize adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the "energy currency" of cells.

text: Such archaeal photosynthesis might have been the earliest form of photosynthesis that evolved on Earth, as far back as the Paleoarchean, preceding that of cyanobacteria (see Purple Earth hypothesis).
en: Such archaeal photosynthesis might have been the earliest form of photosynthesis that evolved on Earth, as far back as the Paleoarchean, preceding that of cyanobacteria (see Purple Earth hypothesis).

text: While the details may differ between species, the process always begins when light energy is absorbed by the reaction centers, proteins that contain photosynthetic pigments or chromophores.
en: While the details may differ between species, the process always begins when light energy is absorbed by the reaction centers, proteins that contain photosynthetic pigments or chromophores.

text: In plants, these pigments are chlorophylls (a porphyrin derivative that absorbs the red and blue spectra of light, thus reflecting green) held inside chloroplasts, abundant in leaf cells.
en: In plants, these pigments are chlorophylls (a porphyrin derivative that absorbs the red and blue spectra of light, thus reflecting green) held inside chloroplasts, abundant in leaf cells.

text: In cyanobacteria, they are embedded in the plasma membrane.
en: In cyanobacteria, they are embedded in the plasma membrane.

text: In economics, inflation is an increase in the average price of goods and services in terms of money, though it originally referred to the increase of the money supply (monetary inflation) that can cause such a universal shift.
en: In economics, inflation is an increase in the average price of goods and services in terms of money, though it originally referred to the increase of the money supply (monetary inflation) that can cause such a universal shift.

text: This increase is measured using a price index, typically a consumer price index (CPI).
en: This increase is measured using a price index, typically a consumer price index (CPI).

text: When the general price level rises, each unit of currency buys fewer goods and services; consequently, inflation corresponds to a reduction in the purchasing power of money.
en: When the general price level rises, each unit of currency buys fewer goods and services; consequently, inflation corresponds to a reduction in the purchasing power of money.

text: The opposite of inflation is deflation, a decrease in the general price level of goods and services.
en: The opposite of inflation is deflation, a decrease in the general price level of goods and services.

text: The common measure of inflation is the inflation rate, the annualized percentage change in a general price index.
en: The common measure of inflation is the inflation rate, the annualized percentage change in a general price index.

text: Changes in inflation are widely attributed to increases in the money supply, fluctuations in real demand for goods and services (also known as demand shocks, including changes in fiscal or monetary policy), changes in available supplies such as during energy crises (also known as supply shocks), significant decreases in interest rates set by the central bank, or changes in inflation expectations, which may be self-fulfilling.
en: Changes in inflation are widely attributed to increases in the money supply, fluctuations in real demand for goods and services (also known as demand shocks, including changes in fiscal or monetary policy), changes in available supplies such as during energy crises (also known as supply shocks), significant decreases in interest rates set by the central bank, or changes in inflation expectations, which may be self-fulfilling.

text: Moderate inflation affects economies in both positive and negative ways.
en: Moderate inflation affects economies in both positive and negative ways.

text: The negative effects would include an increase in the opportunity cost of holding money; incentivizing workers to switch jobs unnecessarily, making labor markets appear tight while average real wages fall; forcing workers into risky wage negotiations to keep pace, as purchasing power erodes between contracts; uncertainty over future inflation, which may discourage investment and savings; and, if inflation were rapid enough, shortages of goods as consumers begin hoarding out of concern that prices will increase in the future.
en: The negative effects would include an increase in the opportunity cost of holding money; incentivizing workers to switch jobs unnecessarily, making labor markets appear tight while average real wages fall; forcing workers into risky wage negotiations to keep pace, as purchasing power erodes between contracts; uncertainty over future inflation, which may discourage investment and savings; and, if inflation were rapid enough, shortages of goods as consumers begin hoarding out of concern that prices will increase in the future.

text: Positive effects include reducing unemployment due to nominal wage rigidity,allowing the central bank greater freedom in carrying out monetary policy, encouraging loans and investment instead of money hoarding, and avoiding the inefficiencies associated with deflation.
en: Positive effects include reducing unemployment due to nominal wage rigidity,allowing the central bank greater freedom in carrying out monetary policy, encouraging loans and investment instead of money hoarding, and avoiding the inefficiencies associated with deflation.

text: Today, most economists favour a low and steady rate of inflation.
en: Today, most economists favour a low and steady rate of inflation.

text: Low (as opposed to zero or negative) inflation reduces the likelihood of economic recessions by enabling the labor market to adjust more quickly and reduces the risk that a liquidity trap prevents monetary policy from stabilizing the economy, while also avoiding the costs associated with high inflation.
en: Low (as opposed to zero or negative) inflation reduces the likelihood of economic recessions by enabling the labor market to adjust more quickly and reduces the risk that a liquidity trap prevents monetary policy from stabilizing the economy, while also avoiding the costs associated with high inflation.

text: The task of keeping the rate of inflation low and stable is usually given to central banks that control monetary policy, normally through the setting of interest rates and by carrying out open market operations.
en: The task of keeping the rate of inflation low and stable is usually given to central banks that control monetary policy, normally through the setting of interest rates and by carrying out open market operations.

text: Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace (née Byron; 10 December 1815 – 27 November 1852), also known as Ada Lovelace, was an English mathematician and writer chiefly known for work on Charles Babbage's proposed mechanical general-purpose computer, the analytical engine.
en: Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace (née Byron; 10 December 1815 – 27 November 1852), also known as Ada Lovelace, was an English mathematician and writer chiefly known for work on Charles Babbage's proposed mechanical general-purpose computer, the analytical engine.

text: She was the first to recognise the machine had applications beyond pure calculation.
en: She was the first to recognise the machine had applications beyond pure calculation.

text: Lovelace is often considered the first computer programmer.
en: Lovelace is often considered the first computer programmer.

text: Lovelace was the only legitimate child of poet Lord Byron and reformer Anne Isabella Milbanke.
en: Lovelace was the only legitimate child of poet Lord Byron and reformer Anne Isabella Milbanke.

text: Lord Byron separated from his wife a month after Ada was born, and died when she was eight.
en: Lord Byron separated from his wife a month after Ada was born, and died when she was eight.

text: Although often ill in childhood, Lovelace pursued her studies assiduously.
en: Although often ill in childhood, Lovelace pursued her studies assiduously.

text: She married William King in 1835.
en: She married William King in 1835.

text: King was a Baron, and was created Viscount Ockham and 1st Earl of Lovelace in 1838.
en: King was a Baron, and was created Viscount Ockham and 1st Earl of Lovelace in 1838.

text: The name Lovelace was chosen because Ada was descended from the extinct Baron Lovelaces.
en: The name Lovelace was chosen because Ada was descended from the extinct Baron Lovelaces.

text: The title given to her husband thus made Ada the Countess of Lovelace.
en: The title given to her husband thus made Ada the Countess of Lovelace.

text: Lovelace's educational and social exploits brought her into contact with scientists such as Andrew Crosse, Charles Babbage, David Brewster, Charles Wheatstone and Michael Faraday, and the author Charles Dickens, contacts which she used to further her education.
en: Lovelace's educational and social exploits brought her into contact with scientists such as Andrew Crosse, Charles Babbage, David Brewster, Charles Wheatstone and Michael Faraday, and the author Charles Dickens, contacts which she used to further her education.

text: Lovelace described her approach as "poetical science" and herself as an "Analyst (& Metaphysician)".
en: Lovelace described her approach as "poetical science" and herself as an "Analyst (& Metaphysician)".

text: Jazz is a music genre that originated in the African-American communities of New Orleans, Louisiana, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
en: Jazz is a music genre that originated in the African-American communities of New Orleans, Louisiana, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

text: Its roots are in blues, ragtime, European harmony, African rhythmic rituals, spirituals, hymns, marches, vaudeville song, and dance music.
en: Its roots are in blues, ragtime, European harmony, African rhythmic rituals, spirituals, hymns, marches, vaudeville song, and dance music.

text: Since the 1920s Jazz Age, it has been recognized as a major form of musical expression in both traditional and popular music.
en: Since the 1920s Jazz Age, it has been recognized as a major form of musical expression in both traditional and popular music.

text: Jazz is characterized by swing and blue notes, complex chords, call and response vocals, polyrhythms and improvisation.
en: Jazz is characterized by swing and blue notes, complex chords, call and response vocals, polyrhythms and improvisation.

text: As jazz spread around the world, it drew on national, regional, and local musical cultures, which gave rise to different styles.
en: As jazz spread around the world, it drew on national, regional, and local musical cultures, which gave rise to different styles.

text: New Orleans jazz began in the early 1910s, combining earlier brass band marches, French quadrilles, biguine, ragtime and blues with collective polyphonic improvisation.
en: New Orleans jazz began in the early 1910s, combining earlier brass band marches, French quadrilles, biguine, ragtime and blues with collective polyphonic improvisation.

text: However, jazz did not begin as a single musical tradition in New Orleans or elsewhere.
en: However, jazz did not begin as a single musical tradition in New Orleans or elsewhere.

text: In the 1930s, arranged dance-oriented swing big bands, Kansas City jazz (a hard-swinging, bluesy, improvisational style), and gypsy jazz (a style that emphasized musette waltzes) were the prominent styles.
en: In the 1930s, arranged dance-oriented swing big bands, Kansas City jazz (a hard-swinging, bluesy, improvisational style), and gypsy jazz (a style that emphasized musette waltzes) were the prominent styles.

text: Bebop emerged in the 1940s, shifting jazz from danceable popular music toward a more challenging "musician's music" which was played at faster tempos and used more chord-based improvisation.
en: Bebop emerged in the 1940s, shifting jazz from danceable popular music toward a more challenging "musician's music" which was played at faster tempos and used more chord-based improvisation.

text: Cool jazz developed near the end of the 1940s, introducing calmer, smoother sounds and long, linear melodic lines.
en: Cool jazz developed near the end of the 1940s, introducing calmer, smoother sounds and long, linear melodic lines.

text: The mid-1950s saw the emergence of hard bop, which introduced influences from rhythm and blues, gospel, and blues to small groups and particularly to saxophone and piano.
en: The mid-1950s saw the emergence of hard bop, which introduced influences from rhythm and blues, gospel, and blues to small groups and particularly to saxophone and piano.

text: Modal jazz developed in the late 1950s, using the mode, or musical scale, as the basis of musical structure and improvisation, as did free jazz, which explored playing without regular meter, beat and formal structures.
en: Modal jazz developed in the late 1950s, using the mode, or musical scale, as the basis of musical structure and improvisation, as did free jazz, which explored playing without regular meter, beat and formal structures.
